# `unreachable-code`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: semantic · Profile: none · Default: error · Fixes: quick fix · Options: none

Reports statements after `return`, `break`, `continue`, `unreachable`, `@panic`,
`@trap`, or `@compileError` in the same block, which AstGen rejects as
unreachable code.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

A statement after `return`, `break`, `continue`, `unreachable`, `@panic`,
`@trap` or `@compileError` in the same block can never run, and AstGen rejects
it as "unreachable code". It usually means a debugging `return` was left in,
or code that was meant to run first ended up after the exit.

## When it fires

It follows AstGen's rule for each block. After a statement that is one of
those diverting expressions (possibly in parentheses), every later statement
is reported until an expression statement other than a declaration,
assignment, `defer`, `errdefer`, `while` or `for`; that statement is the last
one reported. A diversion inside a branch, a nested block or a `comptime`
expression does not count, and neither does a call to a `noreturn` function
such as `std.process.exit`, since the compiler only knows that after analysis.
A file with syntax errors is skipped.

The message, span and "control flow is diverted here" note are the
compiler's. The quick fix deletes every statement after the diversion when
they fill whole lines, unless one of them holds the last use of a binding
declared before them, whose removal would leave that binding unused.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
fn answer() u32 {
    return 42;
    @import("std").debug.print("done\n", .{});
}
```
